articles.title: Hillary Clinton 'looking forward' to Trump's State of the Union, Democratic women staring him down
articles.summary: Hillary Clinton told Rachel Maddow she's eager to see Democratic women stare down Trump at his 2027 State of the Union after the party's midterm wins.
articles.body: Former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton enthusiasm about the prospect of watching President Donald Trump giving his 2027 State of the Union following the midterm elections during an interview that aired Sunday. "When Trump gives his State of the Union, this is what I’m looking forward to, and he has to walk down that aisle," Clinton told MS NOW host Rachel Maddow. "And all these Democratic women are just staring at him. It will be a sight for sore, sore eyes." Maddow interviewed Clinton on Nov. 10, but the conversation aired on Sunday. The interview comes as Democrats are prepared to take control of both the House and the Senate in January. STATE OF PLAY: BLUE WAVE SWEEPS DEMOCRATS INTO POWER, WITH KEY RACES STILL HANGING IN BALANCE Clinton called for accountability as she and Maddow discussed how Democrats could pursue investigations without assistance from the Justice Department. "I think exposure is important, but I also think accountability is important. And so, once we have the exposure about, you know, what the evidence shows, then how do we hold people accountable?" Clinton asked. "Now, in some cases, there may be connected corresponding state criminal actions," she said. "And those can be pursued then by state attorneys general and district attorneys. That’s what happened coming out of Trump’s first term. It was the district attorney here and our state attorney general who actually brought the cases against the Trump business and Trump personally, with the 34 felony-count conviction against him." "So, I think that we also will pay close attention to statutes of limitation, because if there is a, you know, change in the Justice Department in 2029, for example, some of those cases could still be pursued," Clinton added. TOP DEM ON COMMITTEE FIRES BACK AFTER WHITE HOUSE COUNSEL WARNS AGAINST OVERREACH AMID INVESTIGATION THREATS "But I really believe, and we can debate this, but I really believe that we have to hold people accountable," she continued. "I don’t think we’ve done enough of that in the last 20 years." "I do think that there has to be a very carefully analyzed effort to try to figure out, OK, if we're stymied by the Justice Department to actually bring cases and hold people accountable, then do we bide our time? Do we go to the states? We've got to have a bunch of potential options," Clinton said. Maddow also asked whether Clinton believed there was currently a leader of the free world. "Maybe Mark Carney," Clinton responded, referring to Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney. She also said there were strong individual leaders in Europe but added that Europe "has got to get itself organized." RACHEL MADDOW WELCOMES 'BIG FIGHT' BETWEEN SOCIALIST AND MODERATE DEMOCRATS AFTER MIDTERM WINS CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "The American people rejected Hillary Clinton in 2016 partially because of her history of corruption," White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis told Fox News Digital in a statement. "It’s gross that she would call for the weaponization of the Justice Department to target President Trump and his allies. She clearly is still holding a grudge about losing to President Trump in 2016."

articles.title: James Bond: Robert Pattinson to replace Daniel Craig as 007
articles.summary: The 40-year old is best known for his role in films including Twilight, The Batman and The Odyssey.
articles.body:
Robert Pattinson, the British actor known for films such as Twilight and The Batman, has been confirmed as the next actor to play James Bond.

The announcement was made by Amazon MGM Studios in a social media post on Monday, with a picture showing Pattinson in character as 007.

The 40-year-old becomes the seventh actor to play the famous fictional spy and will star in the 26th Bond movie, due to be released in 2028.

In a statement, the London-born actor said: "James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime."

The next Bond film will be directed by Denis Villeneuve and written by Steven Knight, but its title and exact release date have not yet been announced.

In his statement, Pattinson said he was "deeply grateful" to the film's creative team "for their belief in me".

"To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement," he added. "I couldn't be more excited about this partnership and the work ahead with this fantastic team."

The announcement comes after years of intense speculation about who will take over from Daniel Craig in one of the most high-profile - and highly scrutinised - roles in entertainment.

The next 007 film will be the first since long-term Bond producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael G Wilson stepped back and Amazon took creative control of the franchise, after acquiring the series' parent company MGM.

By the time the 26th Bond film is released, it will have been seven years since the last - 2021's No Time To Die - the biggest gap in the franchise's history.

Director Villeneuve is best known for films including the Dune trilogy, Prisoners, Sicario, Arrival and Blade Runner 2049, while writer Knight is known for TV hits Peaky Blinders and House of Guinness, and films including Burnt, Spencer and Locke.

Pattinson has already worked with Villeneuve on Dune: Part 3, where he stars as a new villain, Scytale. The film is released next month.

In a statement reacting to Pattinson's Bond casting, Villeneuve said: "Before anything else, I want to express my deep gratitude to the remarkable actors who joined us on this journey.

"We were surrounded by extraordinary talent, but there can only be one 007. I am overjoyed to welcome Robert Pattinson as our new James Bond.

"He has the timeless soul of 007 and brings a spirit that is completely new. I cannot wait to begin."

Pattinson's casting was also welcomed by Buckingham Palace, with a post on Instagram sharing the news and adding: "Welcome to His Majesty's Secret Service, Mr Bond."

Australian actor George Lazenby, who played James Bond in the 1969 film On Her Majesty's Secret, posted a video on social media welcoming Pattinson to "the most exclusive club in the world".

"Remember to enjoy yourself... Let's see if you'll have 'this never happened to the other fella' moment," Lazenby said.

Several other actors, including Josh O'Connor, Callum Turner and Jack Lowden, were reported to be in the frame for the role as screen tests took place in recent weeks.

But Amazon MGM ultimately went with a household name, choosing a more bankable movie star who is widely seen as a safe pair of hands.

Producers Amy Pascal and David Heyman said the "legacy of James Bond is in great hands with Robert Pattinson".

"His fearlessness as an actor, his self-deprecating wit and his ability to continually reinvent himself make him the perfect Bond for our times."

At 40, Pattinson is one of the older actors who was thought to have auditioned for the role of Bond.

Reports last week suggested Pattinson's deal committed him to playing 007 for three films, rather than the four that had reportedly been discussed with some of the other actors, but that has not been officially confirmed.

Robert Pattinson shot to fame as Cedric Diggory in 2005's Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire

He went on to play vampire Edward Cullen in Twilight, the hugely popular film series based on Stephenie Meyer's best-selling novels.

Pattinson starred opposite Kristen Stewart in five Twilight films in total, which collectively made more than $3bn (£2.2bn) at the box office worldwide.

He has gone on to star in other major films such as 2022's The Batman and Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey, released earlier this year.

But he is also respected within the industry for how many roles he has taken in smaller movies - often independent, experimental or arthouse films.

His other credits include The Lighthouse, Mickey 17, Life, The Drama, Good Time, The Rover, Bel Ami, Primetime, Tenet and The Lost City of Z.

Pattinson follows in the footsteps of only six actors to have played James Bond in the official film series – Sean Connery, George Lazenby, Roger Moore, Timothy Dalton, Pierce Brosnan and Daniel Craig.

Craig appeared in five Bond movies in total, starting with 2006's Casino Royale, and spent 16 years as the secret agent created by author Ian Fleming.

In a statement, Fleming's estate said they were "delighted to welcome Robert Pattinson to the James Bond family".

The next film will mark a new era for the franchise. Amazon purchased MGM for $8.5bn in 2021, which included the rights to distribute James Bond.

Then in 2025, long-time Bond producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael G Wilson agreed to sell creative control of the franchise to Amazon MGM.

Before that, the franchise had been under the Broccoli family's control since 1962's Dr. No, when Sean Connery first starred as Bond.

The Broccoli family preserved the integrity of the character and brand for decades, resisting spin-offs and licensing that some industry experts now expect to see following Amazon's takeover.

articles.title: Israeli opposition accuses Netanyahu of attempted ‘coup’
articles.summary: Rivals call for investigation into reports that PM’s office tried to frame Arab parties.
articles.body:
Israeli opposition leaders have denounced an “attempted coup” by outgoing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

The accusations on Monday came in response to media reports that Netanyahu’s office tried to falsely incriminate members of an Arab-led party before last month’s election, in which the premier’s Likud party was voted out of office.

“As more and more details come to light, it becomes clear: This wasn’t an attempt to disrupt the elections. It was an attempted coup,” opposition leader Yair Lapid said on social media.

Israel’s Channel 12 reported on Sunday that on the eve of the election, Netanyahu’s chief of staff, Ido Norden, called police with a complaint about members of the Ra’am party.

Norden reportedly pointed officers to a purported intelligence source – a former employee of Netanyahu’s office – who provided information that led to the arrest of three Ra’am members. They were later released after police determined the allegations were unfounded .

Israeli newspaper Haaretz reported on Sunday that the head of the Shin Bet domestic security service tried to wiretap leaders of the Arab-led Joint List, but the attorney general refused due to a lack of evidence.

Israeli police said in response that they will “review the decision-making and information-transmission process”. Likud has issued a statement denying the reports.

Following the vote, Netanyahu accused Arab parties of electoral fraud after they gained a record 19 seats in the Knesset.

Yousef Jabareen, the leader of Joint List also decried “an attempted coup by Netanyahu,” and labelled the allegations regarding Shin Bet as “conduct characteristic of dark regimes”.

Ra’am deputy and former police chief Yoav Segalovitz called for an urgent investigation.

“Netanyahu cried out that his election was being stolen, while he himself tried to steal the country and is still trying to do so now,” he wrote on social media.

Netanyahu’s main rival, Gadi Eisenkot, wrote that departing prime minister was “a concrete, direct and immediate threat to Israeli democracy”.

Neither Netanyahu’s bloc nor Eisenkot’s opposition grouping secured the 61 seats required to form a government. However, Joint List and Raam have indicated they support Eisenkot to lead a coalition.

articles.title: At least 17 people killed in 2 mass shootings on the same day in South Africa
articles.summary: JOHANNESBURG — Two mass shootings on the same day in South Africa left at least 17 people dead, but motives were not immediately established for the crimes some 530 kilometers (330 miles) apart, police said Monday.
articles.body: JOHANNESBURG — Two mass shootings on the same day in South Africa left at least 17 people dead, but motives were not immediately established for the crimes some 530 kilometers (330 miles) apart, police said Monday. Eight people were found dead inside a bullet-riddled vehicle in Sweetwaters, outside the city of Pietermaritzburg, according to police, who said they had not immediately identified the victims or any suspects in the shooting Sunday. Nine people were found dead with gunshot wounds inside a shack in the informal settlement of Jeffsville near South Africa’s capital, Pretoria. The shooting reportedly took place Sunday night and no arrests have been made. The Jeffsville case is being investigated by the serious and violent crimes, murder and robbery unit in Gauteng province. The incident is reported to have happened between 10 p.m. and 11 p.m., police said. “Police were alerted at approximately 07:30 this morning, 16 November 2026. On arrival, members found the bodies of nine people, six males and three females, inside the four-roomed shack with gunshot wounds,” said police spokesperson Brenda Muridili. Gauteng Police Commissioner Tommy Mthombeni said the killings could be related to a previous shooting at a nearby informal settlement in Saulsville last year where 12 people were killed and 13 injured. He said one of the people who was killed during the shooting was a “person of interest” in the shooting that happened in Saulsville last year. “We cannot rule out that they may be linked, and may possibly have been a retaliation attack,” Mthombeni said. In the Saulsville case from last year, Mthombeni said police had made a breakthrough and arrested one suspect who is believed to be one of the mass shooters. Gauteng Premier Panyaza Lesufi, who visited the crime scene with the police on Monday, said the provincial government was coordinating with other provincial departments to support the police in their investigations of similar crimes happening in the province, which includes the city of Johannesburg. In the Pietermaritzburg shooting, police spokesperson Robert Netshiunda said some families had come forward to help with identifying the victims but their identities had yet to be confirmed. “It’s still too early to tell what the motive could have been and who could be behind the shooting because we are yet to identify the victims,” said Netshiunda. Several mass shootings linked to criminal gangs have occurred in the past year. In September, three gunmen barged into a small house in an impoverished neighborhood near the coastal city of Durban and opened fire on people attending a party, killing at least 11, including a pregnant woman. In the same month, 17 people were killed and several others wounded when gunmen armed with AK-47 rifles stormed a tavern and opened fire at patrons outside the bar before moving inside and continuing to shoot. In June, multiple shooters killed 12 people in a poor neighborhood in Johannesburg in an attack that police linked to criminal gangs. Also in June this year, an armed gang opened fire in a different low-income neighborhood in Johannesburg, also killing 12 people and wounding at least nine, before fleeing in a minibus. Mthombeni said police had arrested three people in that shooting. They believe that it was linked to territorial battles between rival illegal mining gangs. Two mass shootings two weeks apart in December last year killed 21 people. They also were carried out by multiple gunmen.

articles.title: Photos: California residents gather to watch massive El Nino-fuelled waves
articles.summary: National Weather Service warns that waves of more than 10 metres high could impact some parts of US’s California coast.
articles.body:
Residents have flocked to the waterfront in coastal towns across California to watch giant waves brought on by a potentially historic El Nino climate pattern.

For days, heavy surf has pounded the West Coast of the United States, slamming into piers and inundating coastal areas.

The National Weather Service (NWS) said on Monday that a Pacific storm is expected to bring further rain and snowfall to the western US this week.

A day earlier, the weather service issued a high surf advisory for all beaches along the Pacific Coast, forecasting waves to break as high as 10.7 metres, or 35 feet.

“Stay out of the water, stay off rocks and jetties, and never turn your back on the ocean,” the NWS added, citing the risk of “sneaker waves” — powerful surges of water that can reach higher than expected on a beach, only to pull back into the ocean with potentially deadly force.

Despite the warnings, big-wave watchers gathered at famed lookout points like Mavericks Beach in northern California’s Half Moon Bay.

Mavericks is considered one of the premier big-wave surfing spots in North America, with water cresting as high as a five-storey building. Surfers from across the world have descended on the beach in recent days to catch swells reaching approximately 18 metres, or 60 feet.

Some of the offshore waves have been so strong that they were detected by the Berkeley Seismology Lab, which wrote about the phenomenon on its blog.

“A few miles offshore, there are no beaches for the waves to hit, but their bottoms bang into the continental shelf, where the shallow coastal waters drop off sharply into deeper ocean regions,” the lab explained.

“This impact is strong enough to make all of California shake. In fact, it makes the entire continent wiggle a little.”

While it is typical for California to experience storms in November and December, this year’s heavy rainfall and powerful surf have been turbocharged by a climate phenomenon known as El Nino .

The El Nino pattern occurs when the recurrent warming of the eastern tropical Pacific Ocean releases heat into the atmosphere. Already, experts say ocean temperatures off of California are reaching record levels for this time of year, making the water feel warmer than normal.

El Nino can also alter weather patterns around the world. Scientists and state officials expect an especially strong El Nino this year to result in heavy rain for California in the coming weeks.

“The odds of an unusually wet, and perhaps exceptionally wet, second half of November continue to rise in California,” climate scientist Daniel Swain said in a social media post.

articles.title: Sudanese army air attack kills 13 in western Sudan: Rights group
articles.summary: ‘Preliminary monitoring’ shows women and children killed, homes destroyed in West Kordofan, says Emergency Lawyers.
articles.body:
An air strike launched by the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) has killed at least 13 civilians in the Abu Qalb area of West Kordofan state, according to the Emergency Lawyers rights group.

Warplanes belonging to the military government carried out the attack on the Abu Zabad locality, with the victims including women and children, “according to preliminary monitoring” the legal collective said in a social media post on Monday. Al Jazeera was unable to immediately verify the report.

Several homes were also destroyed in the strike, which took place the previous day, Emergency Lawyers said. The group, which documents human rights violations and crimes in the war between the SAF and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), cited videos circulating of “horrific scenes” of destruction.

“The continued use of indiscriminate airstrikes on residential areas poses a direct threat to civilian lives and constitutes a grave violation of the rules of international humanitarian law,” it said in its statement.

Mohamed Didan, the official spokesperson for the Special Operations Forces that fight alongside the SAF, said on Facebook that his troops had moved through Abu Zabad and “eliminated” RSF positions in West Kordofan.

The war between the army and the RSF, which began in April 2023, has created one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises, according to several aid organisations.

Reports say the war has killed at least 59,000 people, displaced about 13 million and pushed parts of the country into famine.

Much of the fighting is concentrated in Darfur and Kordofan, although it recently shifted towards the Blue Nile province.

Drone warfare has also surged during the war, becoming the deadliest threat to civilians. Both sides are being supplied with drones by countries in the Middle East and beyond, experts have said.

The SAF has gained control over several strategically important villages and localities in West Kordofan recently in a push into the western reaches of the country .

articles.title: 'SNL' joked about daughters being the default caregivers. Women say the 'Sister' sketch is almost too relatable to be funny.
articles.summary: An "SNL" sketch about daughters being the default caregivers for aging parents has struck a nerve with women who recognize the unequal burden, sparking conve...
articles.body:
The elder care service advertised on last week's Saturday Night Live sounded almost too good to be true: round-the-clock attention for an aging parent, without the expense or paperwork.

The catch? It's your sister. And the person getting his life back is her brother.

In " Sister ," a pre-taped sketch that aired during John Mulaney's Nov. 14 hosting appearance, cast member Jane Wickline plays the woman whose life becomes collateral damage in her family's caregiving plan. A text about Dad falling is enough to send her across the country, leaving her job and apartment behind to become a live-in attendant. Her brother, meanwhile, is free to carry on without the responsibility, assured that everything is being handled.

For women who recognize that arrangement, the joke comes with a sting.

The reactions span laughter, anger and apprehension. Liz Plank wrote an entire Substack essay on the sketch, titled "The Sister Sketch is a Documentary." Viva Mogi, who identifies herself as a caregiver, called it "an SNL skit so good, it made me laugh and get triggered at the same time." Nicole Simone claimed it as "one of the most socially progressive, anti-patriarchal sketches ever to air on television," hoping men would reconsider who provides care in their families — and who is simply expected to.

The writing credits drew attention too. Streeter Seidell, who wrote the sketch with Mikey Day and Simon Rich, with an assist from Chase Rosenberg (yes, all four are men), shared it on X with a dedication: "to my sister Heidi."

The assumption then becomes that Heidi is the caregiver that the skit was inspired by. And the men's interpretation of her sacrifices made countless caregivers feel seen.

Kim Elliott, the founder of Gray Monster, a caregiving resource and community, tells Yahoo that she received close to 100 messages and comments after the sketch, overwhelmingly from those who recognized themselves in the role. She appreciates that the labor of caregivers is being recognized, but she's careful about what it means.

"I don't want to confuse that for support," she says.

The men in the commercial aren't confused about the work involved. They simply don't want to do it. As one brother, played by Andrew Dismukes, says of helping his mother in the bathroom: "Sister doesn't [want to] either. But she will, whereas I won't."

Elliott describes the expectations beneath that arrangement as an assumption economy. "We assume someone can take the time off of work. We assume someone else can watch the kids," she says. "We assume someone can coordinate the appointments and absorb the financial consequences."

Historically, that someone has often been a woman, as the sketch so frankly points out. And though the recognition feels good to many caregivers, it can land differently.

Elliott herself is in a respite period between caregiving responsibilities, which she says allows her to appreciate the humor now. "When I was actively caregiving, I think that would have brought up a really different range of emotions," she says. "There's a relief in feeling seen, and there's frustration when everyone recognizes there's a problem, but there's really not a solution or change."

Hence, the reactions from people who said they didn't know whether to laugh or to cry.

There's also something the parody leaves less room for: love.

"What was missing from the SNL skit was that there is so much love behind family caregiving," says Elliott, explaining that wanting help is different from wanting to stop caring for a parent. "What they're really asking is, How am I supposed to keep doing this without sacrificing my own financial security, health, career, family, etc.?"

She doesn't see the answer as pitting daughters against sons. The more useful conversation is about who can take responsibility for what, from financial contributions to meal deliveries for the caregiver. And some of the messages Elliott has received suggest that the sketch has reached people beyond those already doing the work. Men told her their sisters forwarded it, prompting them to subscribe to Gray Monster because they wanted to help.

With Thanksgiving approaching, she suspects that more siblings will receive the clip.

"Family caregivers rarely see their experiences reflected in mainstream culture, which is part of why this resonated so strongly," she says. "Sometimes levity is the best entry point into a difficult subject."

articles.title: Houthi rebel advance in Yemen may further destabilise global economy
articles.summary: The Iran-backed Houthis are gaining ground and their advance could have dangerous consequences, writes the BBC's security correspondent.
articles.body:
The Iran-backed Houthi rebels who seized much of Yemen in 2014 have now forced the army of the internationally recognised government to withdraw from the Red Sea coast in order to defend their interim capital, Aden.

Their advance bodes ill for Yemen's legitimate, internationally recognised government, its Saudi backers and, by extension, much of the rest of the world.

Yemen, a mountainous, heavily armed, intensely tribal and largely impoverished nation, sits at the far south-west corner of the Arabian Peninsula.

The country has two coasts: One faces the Indian Ocean on which sits the once-prosperous trading port of Aden, the other faces the Red Sea and, most importantly, the narrow chokepoint at the southern exit of that waterway - the so-called Bab al-Mandab Strait or, in English, The Gate of Tears.

Whoever controls that strait can threaten any or all maritime traffic passing through from both the Mediterranean and the Red Sea to the Indian Ocean.

In normal times, it accounts for around 12% of global trade, with anywhere between 70 to 150 ships a day making the transit.

But not any more. Although the Houthis say they are no threat to maritime traffic, they are currently at war with Saudi Arabia, making it extremely hazardous for the Saudis to send their oil tankers past the now rebel-controlled coast.

When the US and Israel started a war with Iran in February, Tehran responded by choking off much of the oil trade flowing out of the Gulf through another narrow chokepoint - the Strait of Hormuz. This sent oil prices soaring, boosted inflation and hurt economies everywhere.

The Saudis had a Plan B. Instead of exporting their oil past the dangerous coast of Iran, where their tankers risked being droned or mined by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps, they started pumping it overland through their East-West Pipeline to an export terminal on the Red Sea at Yanbu. This worked for a while.

But then in July a cold truce between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis broke down, that pipeline got hit by drones and the rebels started firing missiles and drones at targets all over Saudi Arabia.

On land, the Houthis seized the initiative and made a lightning dash down the Red Sea coast, sending the Yemeni army into headlong retreat. A brief counter-offensive appears to have failed and the Houthis are now reported to be in full control of the Bab al-Mandab Strait and the nearby offshore islands.

Nicholas Hopton, a former British Ambassador to both Yemen and Iran and now director-general of the UK-based Middle East Association, says: "The decision by the legitimate government of Yemen to prioritise the military defence of Aden at the expense of withdrawing from other areas suggests that the war is not going well for the Saudi-backed [Yemeni] government. And the rest of the world should be worried."

He warns that if the port of Aden – a city of roughly 1.25 million inhabitants – was to fall to the Houthis, it "would undoubtedly precipitate a further escalation in the regional crisis and further fragility in the global economy, catalysed by the US-Iran war".

But Mohammed al-Basha, the Yemeni founder of the US-based risk advisory firm Basha Report, believes the Houthis would struggle to capture the heavily fortified city of Aden.

"Any attempt to seize a densely populated city like Aden would come at a significant human cost," Basha said. "Advancing across the flat coastal plains would also expose Houthi forces to air power."

"For now, the Houthis appear to be seeking a negotiated surrender, hoping to exploit infighting and divisions among southern factions to achieve their objectives without a costly urban offensive."

It is conceivable that the Yemen war will settle into a less dramatic but deeply unsatisfactory stasis - a situation where casualty figures subside yet the country remains split between areas controlled by the Houthis - Iran's Shia allies - and the disparate and often poorly motivated forces of the Saudi-backed Yemeni army.

The former British defence attaché to Yemen, Col Iain Smailes, warned that the recent Houthi advance could trigger a spike in oil prices, as it did when they seized the Bab al-Mandab Strait in September.

He also warns this could have a knock-on effect to security well beyond Yemen's borders.

"By extending their control over the western coastline, the Houthis will increase their ability to smuggle weapons and ammunition from Iran, the Horn of Africa and elsewhere, posing additional threats to the region," Col Smailes said.

"This control will enable both Iran and the Houthis to extend their influence in East Africa and beyond."

articles.title: Women stranded by FAA ground stop buy a Bronco for a 27-hour road trip home
articles.summary: A nationwide ground stop left Tara Harding and her employees stranded. Striking out on planes and trains, she opted to just buy an automobile.
articles.body: Tara Harding and her employees were at the airport trying to get home from a work trip when a nationwide ground stop left them stranded in Charlotte, North Carolina — roughly 1,600 miles from home in Bismarck, North Dakota. She found a $48,000 solution in the form of a new Ford Bronco. Travelers across the U.S. were left scrambling Friday when the Federal Aviation Administration announced that it was grounding all flights as it saw inconsistencies in radar data and communications. Officials said that 20,000 flights were affected in the hourslong ground stop, with 12,000 “unable to recover” after the order lifted. Thousands more flights were either delayed or canceled the next day as airlines scrambled to recover service. Harding, a nurse practitioner who owns a clinic, was ready to get home Friday after being in town for a training with two of her employees. Her group had been at the airport for about 30 minutes when the ground stop occurred. All three women started out trying to find options through Delta Air Lines, but flights were delayed and rebooked until they gave up the idea of getting in the air altogether, Harding said. “In the midst of all of that, though, we’re like, ‘We should probably look at trying to get a rental car,’” Harding said. “So we were trying to look, all three of us at one time, trying to get a rental car. There was zero available rental cars within a four-hour radius.” Greyhound? Sold out. Amtrak? No luck. Uber? No rides to Bismarck. Overwhelmed and out of ideas, Harding called her husband to ask what she should do. He relayed to her an idea from his mom. “She said, ‘Why don’t you guys go buy a car?’” Harding recalled. At that point, the women had been trying unsuccessfully to rebook their flights or find alternatives for more than an hour. So they started texting with a sales agent at a Ford dealership who promised to stay open while they waited 30 minutes for an Uber out of the Charlotte Douglas International Airport. They arrived at 7:45 p.m. and left with a new Bronco less than two hours later. Harding said the process gave her an adrenaline rush. “When we were leaving the airport, I was three-way calling with my husband, the car dealer and my employees, and we were looking at each other like, ‘Is this really happening right now?’” she said. Harding said she knows it sounds “insane,” but she did what she had to do, relying on a problem-solving instinct she tied to being both an entrepreneur and a nurse. “If it was just me, it would have probably been different,” she said. “But I had two employees that needed to get home to their children, and we had patients on Monday morning.” Even picking a Ford Bronco was a rushed decision, she said. Harding and her husband were discussing getting a vehicle with a good resale value, but her husband suggested getting a “fun” car just in case they couldn’t sell it once she got home. “And being a Ford girl, I was like, ‘Broncos look kind of cute and fun,’” she said. Driving the Bronco off the lot, the women drove 27 hours nonstop to Bismarck, making the most of the trip together. They had a rotation on who would sleep and who would drive. “We took turns napping, stopped at gas stations and drive-thrus for food,” she said. Despite the hefty price tag, Harding said she has no regrets about her decision. The women bonded over the journey, and in the end, they have a great story to tell, she added. As for the Bronco, Harding said it’ll be with her for the long haul. “I slept 12 hours when I got home, and when I woke up, my husband had drove it three times, and he said he wants to keep it,” Harding said. “So, we’re keeping it.”

articles.summary: Television host Ryan Seacrest is helping his former high school build a football stadium of its own, bringing a long-standing dream closer to reality for
articles.body: Television host Ryan Seacrest is helping his former high school build a football stadium of its own, bringing a long-standing dream closer to reality for students and the local community in Georgia. The DeKalb County School Board approved the final agreements for the $2.7 million project on November 9, clearing the way for construction at Dunwoody High School. According to reports by The Atlanta Journal-Constitution, Rough Draft Atlanta and USA Today, the project is being supported by a substantial contribution from Seacrest and a community-led fundraising campaign that has raised $1.5 million. The facility, which will be named Seacrest Stadium, is expected to welcome its first football games in August 2027. Seacrest, best known for hosting American Idol and Wheel of Fortune, graduated from Dunwoody High School in 1993 and was also part of its football team. His contribution, reported to be around $1 million, has played a significant role in helping the school move forward with plans that have been discussed for more than two decades.A stadium the school has waited decades forFor years, Dunwoody's football team has had to play its home matches at North DeKalb Stadium, a shared facility used by another local school, Chamblee. Although Dunwoody already has an artificial turf field and a track, its existing seating capacity of around 1,000 was not sufficient to host varsity home games, which require a larger venue.The new development is expected to change that. The renovation will add approximately 2,000 seats, taking the stadium's total capacity to 3,000. The plans also include a press box, upgraded restrooms, a ticket booth, a concession building, improved lighting, fencing and landscaping. Once completed, Dunwoody will become the first school in DeKalb County to have its own on-campus football stadium, allowing students, families and supporters to attend games without travelling to a shared venue. The facility is also expected to accommodate other sporting activities and community gatherings.Community fundraising helped bring the project togetherThe stadium's estimated $2.7 million cost will be covered through a combination of private contributions and community fundraising. The Bring It Home campaign, organised by the Dunwoody High School Community Association, successfully raised its $1.5 million target with support from hundreds of local donors.The remaining funding includes a substantial contribution from Seacrest and his family, reported to exceed $1 million. The school district will oversee the construction process, with BlueGold Construction Management LLC and Fortune-Johnson LLC appointed to handle the project. The DeKalb County School Board's November 9 approval included the final construction agreement and a sponsorship development agreement with the school community association. The approval marks an important step towards turning the fundraising campaign into a functioning stadium.First home games expected in 2027Construction is expected to begin in the coming weeks, with the project scheduled for completion ahead of the 2027 football season. The Wildcats are then expected to play their first official home game on their own school campus, creating an opportunity for new traditions and a stronger connection between the team and its supporters.For a school that has spent years sharing its home-game facilities with another institution, the development represents more than an infrastructure upgrade. articles.title: 'Complete reset' needed to get young people into work, says Milburn review
articles.summary: Alan Milburn's review will call for sweeping reforms to the education, work and welfare systems.
articles.body:
Sweeping reforms are needed to help 440,000 more young people into work, according to former minister Alan Milburn.

Almost one million young people aged 16 to 24 in the UK are not in education, employment or training - or "Neet" - a current rate of 13%, which Milburn wants to fall to around 5% within a decade.

His government-commissioned review, due to be published in full on Tuesday, calls for ministers to intervene from early childhood through to adulthood, funded in part by radical changes to benefits for young adults.

But Helen Whately, Conservative shadow work and pensions secretary, said Milburn's proposals were in parts "too cautious" and too reliant on the "expensive hand of the state".

Many of the review's proposed changes are specific to England, with some welfare and tax measures applying across all home nations.

Milburn, a former Labour health secretary, says extensive change is needed to avoid a "lost generation", and address what he describes as a "moral" crisis.

The review says that, in 2024/25, for every £1 spent helping young people into work or education, £25 was spent on youth benefits.

By 2036, it says the aim should be for that ratio to be £2 on benefits for every £1 on work support.

In order to make change of this scale over the next decade, the review will call for:

A new target of 90% of children to be school-ready with basic life skills by five years old (this figure is now 68% in England, with a current government target of reaching 75% by 2028)

More emphasis on work skills in the school curriculum

Instant access to mental health support without diagnosis

A doubling of the number of young apprentices

At the heart of the changes recommended by Milburn would be a legal entitlement to support, provided through a new "Youth Opportunity Service" in England.

The service would put a young person in touch with a named adviser to help to secure them an apprenticeship, college place, supported employment or a job within four months.

To pay for these reforms, young adults would no longer be eligible for the health top-up of Universal Credit, which provides extra money for people whose health conditions limit their capacity to work, or Personal Independence Payment (Pip), which helps with the extra living costs of having a long-term health condition or disability.

The review's key welfare measures, some of which have already been announced , suggest replacing these benefits for under-25s with a new Youth Allowance at the current base rate of Universal Credit for young people, and a new Additional Cost Allowance to replace Pip.

The minority of young people who are unable to ever work would be supported through a new Severe and Complex Needs Insurance.

Kat, 21, from Devon, currently gets Universal Credit with the health top-up, so is potentially at risk of receiving a much lower level of benefits under the proposed new system.

She has fluctuating physical and mental health problems, including occasional seizures caused by functional neurological disorder, which recently left her needing crutches.

Kat says she "really wants to work", but says she has to rely on welfare support as she has been unable to find a job where she can be employed in a "safe way" because of her health.

Milburn, a Labour MP from 1992 to 2010, says many young people are desperate for opportunity, but that many get knocked back repeatedly.

Josh, 19, has spent three years looking for work while on Universal Credit with the support of youth employment charity Spear.

Although they help him with applications to prospective employers, Josh says "none of them are getting back, and if they do they say you've not got the spot".

Grace Coates, who manages Spear St Helens, says she wants to see "more openness to employing people with limited experience".

Milburn's review will suggest gradually lowering the rate of National Insurance which employers pay for young adult employees to make hiring and keeping them more attractive.

The existing Youth Jobs Grant, where employers receive £3,000 for hiring a young person who has been looking for work for six months, would be retained under the recommendations.

So would the existing Jobs Guarantee, in which the government underwrites the cost of a paid six-month job.

The government has recently announced that young adults will be eligible for the guarantee after 12 months of being on Universal Credit and looking for work, rather than the current 18 months.

The Institute for Fiscal Studies has said reforms will have a greater chance of success if support for young people is balanced with incentives for businesses to hire them.

It said that while cutting benefit entitlements would reduce the cash young people receive immediately, it might take longer for an increase in employment to make up for that for some young adults.

Responding to the Milburn review proposals, the Conservatives' Whately said: "Where Milburn gets it right, we'll back him," but added that the review "fails to bring down the welfare bill, proposes billions more in government spending and won't make the slightest difference for young people stuck on welfare now".

Liberal Democrat deputy leader Daisy Cooper said cutting national insurance for young workers would "only partly undo the damage of Labour's job tax".

She said her party's plans would "shut off the Neets pipeline at source, with 100 hours of real work experience before 18 and a careers coach for every young person".

Reform UK's shadow education secretary Suella Braverman said the 10-year wait to see changes from Milburn's proposals "would be consigning another generation to the scrap heap".

"Reform UK would act now to axe Labour's jobs tax, double the number of apprenticeships and end university scam courses that laden students with debt," she said.

For the Greens, deputy leader Mothin Ali said Milburn's proposals announced so far were "extremely concerning", adding: "There is an alternative to threatening vulnerable people with benefits they need, an alternative to unsuitable short-term work."

articles.title: US Pentagon rejects allegations linking deputy to a Goldman Sachs banker
articles.summary: Pentagon defends Steve Feinberg, amid claims in Bloomberg he encouraged defence contractors to use a specific banker.
articles.body:
The Pentagon has denied reports that Deputy Defense Secretary Steve Feinberg pushed defence contractors to work with a specific Goldman Sachs banker with whom he had longstanding ties.

In a statement sent to Al Jazeera on Monday, the Pentagon said the allegations were “baseless”.

“Any claim that the Deputy directed companies to use Goldman Sachs is categorically false. He worked with financial firms across the industry throughout his entire career,” Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said in the statement.

“He has no favorites, and neither does the Department of War.”

The publication Bloomberg first reported the allegations, citing anonymous sources familiar with the matter.

According to Bloomberg’s report, Feinberg guided defence contractors like Lockheed Martin and RTX towards working with Goldman Sachs banker Jim Donovan during their negotiations with the Pentagon.

Donovan and Feinberg reportedly knew each other. Bloomberg said Donovan has previously worked for the investment firm Feinberg co-founded, Cerberus Capital Management, which claims to oversee $70bn in assets.

Bloomberg’s report has raised concerns about a conflict of interest during the lucrative Pentagon negotiations.

Defence contracts are often million, if not billion, dollar deals. Guiding a company that is competing for a contract to work with a specific banker could be seen as a way of rigging the negotiations.

It would also put the banker in line to potentially receive large commissions from the contracts in question.

According to Bloomberg, both RTX and Lockheed Martin hired Donovan after Feinberg’s suggestion.

The Pentagon, however, has accused Bloomberg of seeking to lend credibility to unsubstantiated allegations.

“Despite the Department’s categorical denial, Bloomberg appears more interested in advancing a baseless smear than establishing the facts. Your sources are playing you, and Bloomberg should know better,” Deputy Pentagon Press Secretary Jacob Bliss told Al Jazeera.

“The Deputy is a man of honor and integrity. Unfortunately, some would rather see him fail than succeed.”

Feinberg was nominated by President Donald Trump for his position in one of the Pentagon’s top posts.

The Senate confirmed him in a vote of 59 to 40, and he was sworn in as the 36th deputy defense secretary on March 17, 2025, according to the Pentagon.

Lockheed Martin and RTX, both aerospace and defence companies, have longstanding ties to the Pentagon.

In August, for instance, the Department of Defense announced a multibillion-dollar deal with Lockheed Martin and another defence giant Northrop Grumman to boost production of parts for the Patriot PAC-3 and THAAD missile interceptor systems.

According to Bloomberg’s reporting, Donovan, the banker, was a part of several deals in recent months involving Lockheed Martin and RTX.

They include a $59bn contract with Lockheed Martin for Patriot missiles and two missile contracts worth approximately $45bn with RTX.

It is unclear who the anonymous sources for Bloomberg’s story might be.

Under Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, the Pentagon has opened multiple investigations into leaks of sensitive information and taken steps to limit journalists’ access to military officials and other Pentagon resources.

articles.title: Caerphilly woman gets addicted to nasal spray after missing warning
articles.summary: Louise Gough says her dependence on decongestant nasal sprays left her feeling like a prisoner.
articles.body:
A woman says her blocked nose left her with a decade-long addiction to decongestant nasal sprays that cost her thousands.

Louise Gough, 30, failed to read the fine print on her over-the-counter Sudafed which warns it is for short-term use only, and ended up addicted.

She came so reliant on the medication she was spraying up to 15 times a day and felt like a "prisoner in her own body".

Sudafed said the safe use of its products was its top priority.

But a consultant surgeon who treats this dependency said the warning should be more prominent on packaging.

Gough, from Caerphilly, estimates she spent about £2,000, secretly buying bottles that cost about £7 because her partner was frustrated by her spending.

"I used it [when I had a cold] and instantly within 10 seconds my nose was unblocked," she said.

"It's partly my fault. I didn't read the box and I didn't realise that you could only use it for a certain amount in a time period.

"No one ever warned me when I bought it. It just turned into a really vicious cycle."

Prolonged use can make congestion worse, so even when Gough did not have a cold, her nose would be blocked and she would use the spray.

She had developed rhinitis medicamentosa, a medication-induced nasal congestion also known as rebound congestion.

"I found myself feeling really anxious if I didn't have a bottle on me," she said.

"This was particularly bad if I was out with my partner as I'd ask him to get me one and he'd be annoyed.

"I laugh about it now but it wasn't funny at the time.

"I felt like a prisoner in my own body and I couldn't get away from it."

Ear, nose and throat (ENT) consultant Vik Veer said decongestant sprays work by temporarily restricting blood flow to the nasal lining.

Prolonged use can trigger a cycle in which the nose becomes increasingly congested as the medication wears off.

"The thing you were doing to try to make you better actually makes you even worse," he said.

"Every ENT surgeon will know about [rebound congestion] and would see this problem almost in every clinic."

Official recommendations are that nasal decongestant sprays containing xylometazoline and oxymetazoline should not be used for more than five consecutive days.

But Veer said he believes rebound congestion can begin much sooner.

"I think the evidence points towards you having problems within three days of using these sprays," he said.

When Gough started taking decongestants, the recommendation was seven days, with the current five-day warning added to packaging in 2026.

When Gough used two bottles in 11 days on her family holiday to Greece she said she knew she had to quit, and stopped taking them three years ago.

"It's like someone has shoved something so far up your nose you physically can't breathe at all," she said.

The first few days off the medication made her feel "claustrophobic in her own body" as she struggled to breathe naturally, she said. But after a month she was finally able to breathe through her nose unmedicated.

But Gough has not regained her sense of taste and smell as strongly as before.

A Sudafed spokesperson said its products followed strict regulatory and industry rules, with usage information provided on packaging, patient information leaflets and its website.

It encouraged anyone with questions about using its products to speak to a GP or pharmacist.

articles.title: Former gin distillery cleared for use as exotic animal sanctuary
articles.summary: A lynx, wolfdog and turkey vulture are among the creatures to be kept at the site in southern Scotland.
articles.body:
Plans to turn the site of a former gin distillery in southern Scotland into a home for exotic animals have been approved.

The Eclipse Animal Sanctuary (EAS) lodged an application to convert the site at Dalton in Dumfries and Galloway to house a variety of species including a wolfdog, lynx, turkey vulture and an American red fox.

The small-scale development will cater for about 20 rescue animals alongside eight pet dogs.

Dumfries and Galloway Council (DGC) approved the plans with a number of conditions, including that the sanctuary was purely private and should not be used for commercial purposes or as a visitor attraction.

The site, a few miles from Lockerbie, opened as a distillery and visitor centre in 2017 with a hut licensed for drinking parties.

Visitor numbers are said to have reached up to 20,000 a year, but it closed in 2023 and was put up for sale for offers over £280,000.

Now it is taking up a very different use after plans to convert it were approved by the local authority.

Council planning officials noted that the animal enclosures were generally formed from converted shipping containers, with external runs formed from mesh fencing, painted black to minimise visual impact.

"All development is within the envelope of the previously developed site and does not extend into the open countryside," a report said.

"There is, therefore, limited visibility from outwith the site."

The officials also noted that the proposal included the keeping of non-native species - some of them predatory.

NatureScot was consulted and offered no objection and the council concluded that the conversion of the site could go ahead.

A representative of the sanctuary previously told the BBC it understood that people might have questions about keeping such animals near neighbouring farms.

However, it stressed that the predatory animals were housed in "specially-designed, secure enclosures".

The enclosures are also inspected on site every day as well as annually as part of the conditions of their Dangerous Wild Animal licence.

articles.title: EU agrees to resurrect cooperation deal with Syria
articles.summary: Decision aims to bolster bloc’s ties with Damascus following the collapse of Assad’s government in December 2024.
articles.body:
European Union foreign ministers have agreed to revive a nearly 20-year-old cooperation deal with Syria, as the bloc presses to strengthen ties with the war-scarred country.

“Syria needs investment and a successful transition,” EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said on Monday.

“The aim is to give Europe and Syria a framework for trade, political dialogue and closer cooperation as soon as possible.”

The EU-Syria association agreement was first made in 2008 under then-President Bashar al-Assad, but it was never fully signed by either side, owing to concerns over the Assad government’s human rights record.

Kallas said EU foreign ministers meeting in Brussels had “supported moving ahead” with that deal and launching talks for an updated one.

A discussion paper prepared by the bloc’s diplomatic service ahead of the meeting outlined one of Brussels’ most ambitious efforts yet to normalise ties with Syria, less than two years after Assad’s fall .

Kallas said diplomats would now work through the technical and legal details to finalise the agreement, which would create a framework for free trade, political dialogue and broader cooperation between Brussels and Damascus.

“Everybody said that we need to engage with Syria because if we don’t engage, then this vacuum will be filled by other players,” Kallas said.

Kallas said the EU would set out new conditions for Syria to secure an updated deal.

“We should have clear conditionality regarding human rights,” she said.

“We should have also the nonrecognition of occupied Ukrainian, Georgian territories that they have recognised under Assad’s regime.”

The move is the latest in the 27-nation bloc’s efforts to bolster ties with Damascus and its new leader, President Ahmed al-Sharaa.

The EU in 2025 removed its crushing sanctions on Syria’s economy in a bid to help its recovery after almost 14 years of civil war.

At the start of 2026, Brussels announced a two-year funding package worth 620 million euros ($680m) for the country.

The 53-year-long rule of the Assad family ended on December 8, 2024, after an 11-day offensive that took Syria and the world by surprise.

It also halted a lengthy civil war that left lasting scars on the country and saw some 6.8 million Syrians, about one-third of the population, flee abroad .

More than one million Syrian refugees have already returned home since Assad’s fall, while millions more among the diaspora weigh the decision to do the same and rebuild their lives in their homeland.

articles.title: U.K. leader Andy Burnham says Brexit hasn’t worked ahead of a reset summit with the EU
articles.summary: LONDON — British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Monday that it’s time to admit that Brexit has not delivered for the U.K. and that the country needs a much closer relationship with the European Union to combat growing isolationism around the world.
articles.body: LONDON — British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Monday that it’s time to admit that Brexit has not delivered for the U.K. and that the country needs a much closer relationship with the European Union to combat growing isolationism around the world. He compared the outcome of Britain’s divorce from the EU, triggered by a 2016 referendum, to the Hans Christian Andersen fairy tale “The Emperor’s New Clothes,” in which no one is willing to tell the ruler that he is, in fact, naked. “Well, I do try to say things as I see them,” Burnham said in a speech on foreign policy at the Lord Mayor’s Banquet in London’s financial district. “The Brexit we were given has not worked. We have lost more than we gained.” Seeking to draw a line under a decade of political turmoil that has made him Britain’s seventh prime minister since 2016, Burnham said the U.K. was back on the world stage. He argued the country is well positioned to lead in an era of renewed international cooperation because of its experience since 2016. “Brexit was the first domino to fall in a global move toward more isolationism and protectionism,” he said. “It was exactly what our enemies wanted. Russia wanted disunity within NATO and a weaker Europe.” Burnham spoke ahead of a U.K.-EU summit in Brussels on Friday that is a key step in his pledge to reset relations with the 27-nation bloc, a decade after the U.K.’s vote to leave and six years after the departure in 2020. It is expected to seal a trade deal for food and drink, agreements on energy and emissions trading and a plan to let young people work for limited periods across Britain and the EU. Burnham argued that the promise of the pro-Brexit campaign that Britain would “take back control” of its borders, laws and economy had not been delivered. Trade with EU countries is down sharply, and estimates of the economic damage range from 4% to 8% of the U.K.’s gross domestic product, he said. Most economists agree that Brexit has hurt the British economy, but U.K. politicians have been wary of reopening a painful debate. Not Burnham. He said that soon after the summit, he will open a national conversation on Britain’s long-term relationship with the bloc. His spokesman Tom Wells said Monday that “no assumptions are being made” and “the British public will be the boss of any outcome.” Until the next national election, Burnham remains bound by the pledge of Keir Starmer, whom he replaced as center-left Labour Party leader and prime minister, not to rejoin the bloc’s tariff-free customs union or frictionless single market for goods, services and workers. Erasing that pledge would reignite a subject that split the country: The referendum vote was 52% in favor of leaving the EU and 48% in support of staying in. Brexit-backing former Conservative Prime Minister Boris Johnson said if Burnham tried to take Britain back into the EU, “people will wake up to what is going on. They won’t want it, and he won’t succeed.”

articles.title: China is hosting the world's leaders in Shenzhen's AI wonderland. Here's what they won't see
articles.summary: Drive away from Shenzhen's tech-flecked skyline and you will run into the challenges confronting Xi's China.
articles.body:
At 27, Huang Shihua is living the Chinese Dream.

He works as an engineer for a leading humanoid robot company in Shenzhen. The sprawling south-eastern metropolis is touted by China as the origin story for a high-tech future powered by artificial intelligence, robotics and home-grown innovation.

Drones soar across the sky to deliver your dinner, driverless taxis play relaxing music as you journey to your destination, and robots don't just hand you a cappuccino - they explain the origin of your coffee beans.

"We have created a miracle in Shenzhen," Huang says, surrounded by humanoid robots making coffee and playing chess. "Many young people from across China, full of passion and dreams, have flocked here."

Now they all spend their days figuring out ways to make robots smarter.

The Chinese call Shenzhen the "city of dreams". The moniker suits it: one of China's wealthiest, it is close to Hong Kong and the place where the country's explosive growth took off decades ago.

Its manufacturing inventory mirrors China's rise: cabbage patch dolls, then TVs, later iPhones, electric vehicles, drones and now the robots, which are drawing Huang and a new generation of Chinese ambition.

The "miracles" these young engineers are chasing are central to Xi Jinping's bold vision for China. So where better to show it off than Shenzhen, which will be centre-stage when US President Donald Trump, Russian leader Vladimir Putin and others arrive for a global economic summit this week.

And yet there is another side to this flashy, coastal city, a side that they will not get to see. Drive away from towering skyscrapers towards Shajing and Songgang, once the source of much of the world's electronics, and you will run into the challenges confronting Xi's China.

"Everyone feels life is hard," one construction worker tells us. "Lots of factories have relocated and workers lost their jobs."

China remains exceptionally good at making things - and Shenzhen is proof of that. But the city also holds the evidence for what ails the world's second-largest economy. The property crisis is not over, denting confidence in the future. This is one of China's most expensive cities but even here, our taxi driver tells us, his house is now only worth a third of its original price.

A weak property market and sluggish consumer spending mean many households are buying less. Factories are increasingly relying on exports while many manufacturers have cut production, downsized, automated or moved elsewhere in search of cheaper labour.

The result is a growing number of workers turning to temporary jobs in the gig economy, often with lower pay and fewer benefits.

"Shenzhen is not a magic place," says one delivery driver in his 40s, unwilling to give his name.

"Some say there is gold everywhere in Shenzhen, but it's not like that anymore. It's not a city where you can come and thrive. If you don't work hard, you won't have anything."

The BBC spent several days in Shenzhen exploring these two very different sides of China's progress: on the one hand is the dazzling promise of AI, and on the other are the anxieties of workers who worry if there will be room for them in the future it creates.

Wednesday is sandwich and bubble tea day in the offices of DexForce Technologies.

The elevator is packed with young engineers and developers headed to the right floor for the free carbs and sugar that will fuel their afternoon. They jostle past their creations en route: human-sized, yellow robots whose limbs fill every available corner.

"I believe that in a decade, robots will be able to better serve humanity by taking on highly repetitive or even dangerous tasks," Huang says. That could be anything from serving coffee to working in mines, and they are being trained for all of that in this laboratory for the future, where machines flail, jerk or lurch into motion as they learn to behave.

To him, "Shenzhen is another 'America'. Because, much like in the US, many young people have been able to realise their dreams and earn the wealth they desire."

This is what Xi wants to hear as he pushes China to lead the world in advanced tech. Shenzhen has indeed long been a place for seeking opportunity but Huang and his colleagues want to do much more. They don't simply want to continue China's manfuacturing supremacy. They want to transform it.

Beyond making "our lives more convenient and comfortable", Huang sees AI as helping "the entire world become one family - a global village. AI has the potential to foster equality and the prospect of AI-driven equality is, to me, the most exciting possibility of all."

Smiling enthusiastically, he explains how he hopes that robots can help emerging economies across Africa and South East Asia catch up by reshaping their production lines too.

This tech-charged optimism, which is everywhere in the building, jars with the uncertainty elsewhere in Shenzhen, where robots are nowhere to be found. Yet. But that's just the first of the differences.

In Huang's side of the city, tech and finance workers stroll to the office after a morning workout, sipping coffee that probably cost more than 30 yuan ($4.50; £3.40).

On the other side, scooters whizz through streets piled high with goods being shuttled between factories as vendors sell whole breakfast plates of spicy noodles for under 3 yuan.

Outside one of the city's tallest skyscrapers, 50-year-old Ms Lu has a phone to her ear and a pen in her right hand while grabbing a bag with her left from a delivery driver.

She shouts four key numbers at her co-worker: instructions for another Chinese woman who is waiting to take the delivery up the elevator to someone sitting at their desk.

This is the lunchtime rush outside SEG plaza, home to 70 storeys of thousands of tenants. Lu used to be one of them. "I ran a small business on the second floor. I sold circuit boards," she says. "But it's getting so hard to do business these days and the rental fees got higher."

Often likened to China's Silicon Valley, Shenzhen has seen rents soar with the influx of new capital, squeezing out smaller, more traditional businesses. At 50, Ms Lu couldn't find another job until the delivery drivers came to her with a plan.

The wait for the elevator can take half an hour – wasted money for a driver trying to fill as many orders as possible. So Ms Lu became a new layer in the ever-evolving gig economy.

"The delivery drivers bring food here to the building entrance. We pick it up and take it upstairs. The drivers pay us 2 yuan per order," she explains, always on the move. Delivery drivers earn between four to eight yuan per order, so Ms Lu gets a decent cut of their earnings.

"The lunch peak time only lasts two or three hours… if they use our service, they can get more orders done, and we can earn some money as well. But the market is bad. These days I only earn around 200 yuan per day."

An estimated 200 million Chinese workers, roughly 40% of the urban labour force, now depend on some form of gig work. Many delivery drivers in Shenzhen tell us they chose temporary work because there are fewer opportunities at factories than before.

"We need to adapt to the situation we find ourselves in," one driver told us, "rather than waiting for it to adapt to our needs." A group of them are waiting outside the gates of an e-cigarette factory to make industrial deliveries.

Others nod in agreement. Another driver says he has little choice: "I have two children to raise and I can't stop working. I don't have time to think about anything else."

Permanent jobs often require contributions to social security and pension, which reduces take-home pay. But gig work means more cash in hand and flexibile hours.

"Most workers prefer jobs with a fixed, shorter-term duration. It allows them the flexibility to resign and leave whenever they choose; they have no desire to become permanent employees," says job agent Li Xiaohe.

Increasingly, he puts up boards on pavements advertising temporary factory jobs that pay around 22 yuan an hour for assembling small electronics.

Although agents also appear to be in a shrinking pool, with several former shop fronts shuttered: yet another sign of the downturn in traditional manufacturing.

"Our business is perhaps not as optimistic as it once was," Li admits. "We can feel the effects of Shenzhen going through a transformation."

Drones buzz above the lush grounds of a purpose built "talent park" along the city's waterfront, dipping and darting as they deliver meals to a dedicated platform. Phones held high, tourists capture them landing with their lunch.

"This is amazing. The technology is just great. I wish we had this back at home," exclaims one Canadian tourist. Our coffee order - for a five-yuan delivery - arrives in just over 15 minutes, the drone landing seamlessly so I can pick up my order.

"I heard that many years ago, Shenzhen was a fishing village," says Anle, who is visiting from Vietnam. "Ha – no more fishing village," he laughs as he orders milk tea to be delivered by drone for him and his wife.

For all the ingenuity on display, it feels more like a demonstration of what is possible rather than a mundane reality. The deliveries, which are only possble in certain locations, stop at 20:00 local time. The driverless cars, which need a separate app to order, are also a novelty – they even offer you a massage when you are on your way.

At night, in the glow of a thousand dancing lights, the drones take on a different role. They fly above the park warning people to behave and not cause trouble.

Far from the glittering skyline, workers gather around plastic tables outside restaurants serving cheap hotpot and seafood skewers.

There are more expensive restaurants along the street, but they too have taken a hit. One owner told us business is down by more than 70% as workers are hesitant to splurge on dinner.

Many of them have spent decades here, including 58-year-old construction worker Mr Wu. He arrived in Shenzhen from Sichuan in the 1990s not long after China opened the city up to foreign businesses.

He was among millions of migrants from poorer provinces who came to work on production lines or build skyscrapers. They are still coming.

All the people we spoke to came from elsewhere. They often labour up to 14 hours a day and live in shared dormitories, sustained by the prospect of stable work and decent pay to send home to their families.

For these workers, the Covid pandemic, when Chinese manufacturing hit a record low, appears to have been the first turning point.

"After Covid, our salary dropped by at least a third," Mr Wu recalls, after which wages never fully recovered.

"I will continue to work," he adds. "As long as you keep working, you will have an income. More salary or not? It doesn't matter. As long as you keep working, you will have an income. If the economy slows down, we all slow down. If it grows, we all get better."

For all these decades, Shenzhen lived up to its bargain: work hard and your life would improve.

But now, in a city that is being redefined by automation and AI, that old promise feels less secure.

articles.title: Customers report outages at Chase, Bank of America and Wells Fargo
articles.summary: Chase Bank, the largest US bank, said a software bug might be causing the issue, but that it was not "systemic'" or "cyber-related".
articles.body:
Thousands of customers at major US banks, including JP Morgan Chase, Wells Fargo and Bank of America, have reported trouble accessing services.

Chase Bank - the largest banking institution in the US - said a "software bug" in its hardware systems may have been behind the glitch and noted the impacts may have affected other banks. It added the issue was "temporary" and not "systemic" or "cyber-related".

Problems appeared to be easing for many customers by early Monday evening.

The issue comes after a string of unrelated technical problems, including a massive Microsoft outage , a network failure that grounded all US flights , and United Airlines reporting a "widespread system outage".

Problems started on Monday afternoon. There were almost 5,000 reports of problems with Chase Bank's services, according to the Downdetector website.

Clients reported issues accessing their online accounts, viewing balances and performing transactions, like bank transfers and wire transfers, according to the BBC's US media partner CBS News.

A Chase Bank customer in Texas told the outlet that he could not deposit a check at a Dallas branch on Monday, reporting that he was told his transaction could not be completed. He said a bank teller told the customer in front of him that the "system was down" but did not provide additional details.

Microsoft says services fully restored after day-long global outage

Microsoft outage 'stark reminder' of how much we rely on tech

Chase Bank told its customers that "some transactions are taking longer than usual to complete" but they still had "access to their accounts and funds".

The bank, a subsidiary of JP Morgan Chase, serves more than 86m customers at 5,000 branches across the US, as well as 7.4m small businesses, according to the company's webpage. It is also the top credit card issuer in the US.

The exact nature of the bug was unclear. The BBC has contacted Chase Bank.

Bank of America customers had issues at ATMs and using mobile banking services online, while US Bank customers reported issues with their online accounts and the bank's mobile app, CBS reported.

Customers using another institution, US Bank, also reported issues transferring funds and Wells Fargo customers said they had problems signing into their accounts, getting account balances and making transactions.

US Bank said some its systems were not directly affected but clients using the Zelle, a digital payment platform, received error messages saying their payments could not be sent.

Zelle has said its service is "operating as it should" and issues at other banks could be affecting payments.

Customers also reported issues with Truist, PNC and Capital One but all these companies told the BBC they have not been impacted.

As of 18:00 EST (23:00 GMT), Chase, Bank of America and US Bank had seen a fall in the number of reported outages.

Just as the banking issue affected US customers on Monday, United Airlines confirmed a "widespread system outage", which it described as "a technology issue affecting departing flights".

The Chicago-based airline did not say what is believed to have caused the issue, but a spokesperson said it is not related to cybersecurity.

The issue did not appear to be affecting any other airlines.

The United issue is separate from the one that hit the US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) , but comes as other industries report different outages around the US.

On Friday, the FAA issued a rare nationwide a ground stop, halting all US air travel due to a telecommunication and network upgrade issues.

The halt lasted just over four hours, but the knock-on effect continues to snarl US air travel.

articles.title: Meet Sonny Gallardo, 14, who built a five-person lawn care business in Kansas after starting at age 10; thieves stole $20,000 in equipment, but strangers raised over $36,000 to help him rebuild
articles.summary: Sonny Gallardo, a 14-year-old from Prairie Village, Kansas, built Sunnyside Jobs LLC from a sixth-grade leaf-raking business into a five-person lawn care
articles.body: Sonny Gallardo, a 14-year-old from Prairie Village, Kansas, built Sunnyside Jobs LLC from a sixth-grade leaf-raking business into a five-person lawn care operation. On October 30, someone stole his 10-foot trailer, five mowers, two weed eaters, two blowers, and other equipment from his work vehicle, leaving him with about $20,000 in losses, according to PEOPLE, KCTV5, and the GoFundMe campaign set up to help him recover.The theft happened just before Halloween, and Gallardo had not yet secured insurance coverage for the business. Within days, however, more than 800 strangers had donated over $36,000 to help him replace what was taken, turning a devastating loss into a story about community support. Read more about it, as per the reports, here:How the business beganGallardo started doing lawns after school in the fall of sixth grade. His grandfather would drop him off with the tools he needed to go door to door raking leaves, and those small jobs eventually grew into mowing lawns.Over four years, the business expanded enough to support a five-person crew. Gallardo upgraded his trailer twice and accumulated equipment worth about $20,000, all through work he did himself.He has said that he loves the work because it gives people joy and gives him joy too. “I love making people happy,” he told KCTV5. That motivation is part of what has kept him going even after the theft.What was stolenThe theft happened in the middle of the night on October 30. Someone unhooked Gallardo’s 10-foot trailer, which had all five mowers on it, and took everything. They also cleared out the back of his work vehicle.The stolen items included five mowers, two weed eaters, and two blowers, along with other equipment. Gallardo said the total value was about $20,000, and that it took him three years to acquire all of it.Ring doorbell video captured the theft, and the Prairie Village Police Department is investigating. As of November 13, no arrests had been made, and police said the only description of the suspect’s truck was that it was dark colored.Why insurance did not cover itGallardo’s family said the business was in the process of getting insured when the theft happened. One insurance company denied coverage because Gallardo also does power washing, and he was working with another insurer when the theft occurred.That timing meant the loss was not covered. The GoFundMe campaign was created to help replace the stolen equipment and rebuild Sunnyside Jobs.The situation highlights a common challenge for young business owners. Insurance can be complicated, especially when a business offers multiple services, and delays in securing coverage can leave a company exposed when something goes wrong.The community respondedGallardo’s mother, Monica Gallardo, started the GoFundMe to help him rebuild. The campaign quickly gained traction, with donations pouring in from neighbors and strangers alike. As of November 13, the campaign had raised $36,536 from 836 donors, well beyond the $20,000 goal, as per the reports. The outpouring of support surprised Gallardo, who said he was speechless and still could not believe it.“I’m just thankful to God for all these people who are donating money,” he told KCTV5. That gratitude reflects the emotional weight of the moment, where a community came together to help a young entrepreneur recover.Gallardo is still workingDespite the loss, Gallardo has not stopped working. He is still available for jobs in Prairie Village, and he has made it clear that the theft will not stop him.“Nothing is going to put me down,” he told KCTV5. “I mean, you can try your best, but I’m never going to go down. I love this stuff too much. It’s been my dream since I was little.”That resilience is part of what has drawn people to his story. A teenager who built a business from scratch, lost nearly everything overnight, and still kept working is a powerful example of determination.What comes nextThe GoFundMe funds will help Gallardo replace the stolen mowers and gear. The goal is to rebuild Sunnyside Jobs so it can continue serving customers and supporting the crew that depends on it.Police are asking residents to watch for large amounts of lawn equipment in yards or being sold online, in case the stolen items turn up.For Gallardo, the support has been more than financial. It has been a reminder that the work he has put into his business is seen and valued by others, and that even a difficult setback can become a moment of connection.You use AI every day.
