articles.title: Paraguay ex-president moved to military jail amid special treatment reports
articles.summary: Santiago Pena has been accused of corruption following the collapse of Ueno Bank earlier this month.
articles.body:
Paraguay’s former President Santiago Pena has been transferred to a military prison on a judge’s orders, following reports that he was granted special amenities while awaiting trial for a financial corruption scandal.

On Monday, Judge Osmar Legal ordered Pena to be moved from the Presidential Escort Regiment, a military base in the capital city of Asuncion.

There, media reports indicated he had a large dining room, furnishings, a private gym and a bathroom, sparking public backlash.

His new lodgings are inside Vinas Cue military prison. Pena, however, is to be held separately from the facility’s other prisoners for his safety.

Allegations against the former president are at the centre of a corruption scandal related to the collapse of a major financial lender, Ueno Bank, used by more than half of the country’s adult population.

The political crisis erupted into the public spotlight on November 3, when Paraguay’s central bank took control of Ueno after declaring it insolvent.

In doing so, it froze account activity for nearly three million people. In the months before its collapse, Ueno held roughly $850m in public funds, including money for retirement pensions.

The scandal led to the end of Pena’s presidency. A member of the conservative Colorado Party, a leading force in Paraguay’s politics, Pena saw his political allies distance themselves from him in the wake of the lender’s collapse.

His attempts to resign were rejected, as Paraguay’s Congress instead pursued impeachment proceedings against him. He was removed from office on November 6.

As criminal investigations unfolded, scrutiny fell on Pena’s role as a shareholder in Ueno’s parent company. Pena has denied wrongdoing and said he sold his shares in 2025.

Prosecutors, however, have accused Pena of using his position in office to direct public funds to the bank while it made insider loans to owners.

He faces charges including breach of trust, criminal association and administration for personal gain. Angry protests accompanied Pena’s removal , and he was ordered to be held in pretrial detention.

His former vice president, Pedro Alliana , has since been sworn in to lead Paraguay’s executive branch.

In a news conference on Monday, Alliana said he had dismissed a military official, Colonel Jose David Daiub, accused of giving Pena special treatment while in detention.

“Our priority is to guarantee the country’s stability, restore confidence, and provide concrete and rapid solutions,” said Alliana.

Paraguayans, he added, “deserve to know the truth”. Pena’s transfer to a military prison came on his 48th birthday.

articles.title: One of the victims of the Washington, D.C., gym shooting is a gun control activist
articles.summary: One of the people wounded in last week’s Washington, D.C., shooting is an anti-gun activist from Minnesota who was walking her daughter’s dog at the time, the daughter said Monday.
articles.body: One of the people wounded in last week’s Washington, D.C., shooting is an anti-gun activist from Minnesota who was walking her daughter’s dog at the time, the daughter said Monday. Susan Hamerski, 67, was shot in the temple. She is in stable condition and “past the life-threatening part, but she still has a long way to go,” her daughter, Madeleine Hamerski, said. Hamerski was one of five people hit by gunfire on Thursday after disgruntled doctor Matt Wade Lambert, 55, fatally shot the manager of his condo building in a gym located on the ground floor. He then ran upstairs to his penthouse and began spraying bullets from his balcony at the people below, according to police. One of those bullets struck Hamerski. Family friend Tina Wilcox, who is acting as the family’s spokesperson, said Hamerski’s injuries “are extensive.” “Right now, she is unable to speak or swallow” and is breathing with the help of a ventilator, Wilcox said. “The bullet entered her temple and exited through her jaw and did a lot of damage.” Hamerski will need multiple surgeries to restore function to her jaw and tongue, as well as reconstructive surgery to repair her face, Wilcox said. “Then she’ll need months of rehabilitative therapy,” she said. Hamerski worked for six years with the grassroots advocacy movement Moms Demand Action, which fights for public safety measures to protect communities from gun violence, her daughter said. But the reason she was in Washington was that her daughter was on her honeymoon and she was dog-sitting the newlywed’s dog, Wrigley. “She was walking Wrigley when she was shot,” her daughter said. Law enforcement responded quickly to Thursday’s shooting, which took place in the trendy Logan Circle neighborhood, just a mile from the White House. But by the time they arrived on the scene, Lambert had barricaded himself inside his condo and was shooting through the door, police said. He then fatally shot himself, officials said. After she underwent surgery, and while recovering in the intensive care unit, Hamerski found the strength to write a brief note to her family in which she stressed her support for gun control, her daughter said. “She was coming out of surgery and it came out kind of fuzzy, but the family knew what she was trying to say. ... The point being the gun violence is not simply a political issue, a criminal issue, or a matter of individual tragedy,” Wilcox said in a text message. “It’s also now a public health crisis because it’s happening so often.” Previously, Hamerski worked for the Minnesota Department of Health and served on the board of the Illusion Theater in Minneapolis, her family said. She is also a poet.

articles.title: Ethiopia and Sudan accuse each other of backing armed fighters as fears of a wider conflict grow
articles.summary: CAIRO — Tensions between Sudan and Ethiopia have escalated, with each accusing the other of supporting armed groups that wage war within its borders, undermining efforts to resolve the conflicts that have gripped the two neighboring African countries.
articles.body: CAIRO — Tensions between Sudan and Ethiopia have escalated, with each accusing the other of supporting armed groups that wage war within its borders, undermining efforts to resolve the conflicts that have gripped the two neighboring African countries. Sudan’s military says Ethiopia has allowed Sudanese paramilitary forces battling the army to use its territory to set up camps, launch drones and stage cross-border attacks. In early November, the Sudanese military filed complaints against Ethiopia with the U.N. Security Council and the African Union’s Peace and Security Council, saying it submitted evidence to back up its case. Within days, Ethiopia expelled six staff members of a Sudanese Consulate and ordered the mission closed. Ethiopia says the Sudanese military supports rebels fighting Ethiopian federal forces in its Tigray border region, where fighting returned in September, shattering a 2022 peace agreement. Each country denies the other’s accusations, and The Associated Press could not independently verify their claims. But the tensions — compounded by competing regional alliances and contentious issues over resources and disputed territory — risk a wider regional conflict. Jervin Naidoo, a senior political economist at Oxford Economics Africa, told the AP that the situation “raises the risk that instability inside Ethiopia becomes another front in Sudan’s war — and vice versa.” Here’s a closer look at what’s behind the escalation and how it could impact the wider region: Sudan’s military says Ethiopia backs Sudanese paramilitary forces Sudan was plunged into war in April 2023, when long-simmering tensions between the army and paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, or RSF, turned into all-out fighting. So far, at least 59,000 people have been killed, according to Armed Conflict Location & Event Data, or ACLED, a conflict monitor, though aid groups warn that the real number is likely much higher. Some 13 million people have been displaced. The war, now in its fourth year, has left the Sudanese military in control of the north, east and central regions, including Sudan’s Red Sea ports and its oil refineries and pipelines. The RSF and its allies control western Darfur and parts of Kordofan along the border with South Sudan — both regions rich in oil fields and gold mines. The latest flashpoint in the war is in Sudan’s Blue Nile province, which borders Ethiopia. In late August, the Humanitarian Research Lab, a Yale University research group that uses satellite imagery to monitor conflicts, found an increase in military vehicles and equipment at an Ethiopian military base in Asosa, a city near the Sudanese border. Based on satellite imagery, the Yale group confirmed the buildup was linked to the RSF. “The RSF is engaged out of Ethiopia ... to try to open a second front,” said Nathaniel Raymond, head of the research group. Ethiopia says Sudan’s military backs the Tigray rebels Fighting resumed in September in Ethiopia’s northern Tigray region, where the Tigray People’s Liberation Front, or TPLF, and Ethiopian federal troops fought between 2020 and 2022, when a peace deal was signed. Later that month, Ethiopia’s army chief, Field Marshal Birhanu Jula, suggested that Sudan, Eritrea and Egypt were supporting rebel troops who at the time had captured several strategic towns. The allegations drew sharp denials from the three neighbors. In early November, Ethiopia expelled the six staff members of Sudan’s mission in Asosa and closed the consulate. Naidoo, from Oxford Economics Africa, warned that continued fighting in Tigray could divert Ethiopia’s attention from its myriad other issues and increase the risk of weapons and fighters flowing across the border with Sudan. “All the ingredients are present for an intensifying proxy war between Ethiopia and Sudan that further destabilizes both countries,” said Alan Boswell, Horn of Africa project director at the International Crisis Group. Unresolved disputes, competing political alliances and a flashpoint border Relations between Sudan and Ethiopia have deteriorated since late last year, when the RSF established camps on Ethiopian territory, according to Ladd Serwat, senior Africa analyst at ACLED. In October, a drone strike blamed on the RSF hit a gathering of displaced people on Sudan’s border with Ethiopia and killed 41, said the Emergency Lawyers rights group, which tracks the war in Sudan. “Sudan and Ethiopia don’t operate in a vacuum; their relations amid these current domestic conflicts are shaped by external backers,” said Serwat, adding that Ethiopia is allied with the United Arab Emirates while Sudan is part of an Egypt-Eritrea regional alliance. Turkey has been balancing, backing both Khartoum and Addis Ababa, he said. Serwat added that Ethiopia’s support for the RSF is primarily logistical, while the UAE remains its main backer, funding camps and supplying weapons. The UAE has repeatedly denied any involvement in Sudan’s war. Other issues have also marred relations, including Ethiopia’s construction of a huge dam — Africa’s largest dam — on the Blue Nile, the main Nile River tributary. The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam near the Ethiopia-Sudan border cost about $5 billion and was completed in 2025, aiming to boost Ethiopia’s power production and economy. But it has triggered a dispute with Egypt and Sudan, which have called for a legally binding agreement on the dam’s filling and operation to protect their own water resources. Another issue is the disputed border region of Al-Fashaga, where Ethiopian farmers have long cultivated the area’s fertile soil, according to the International Crisis Group. In late 2020, Sudanese troops moved in to reassert control over the area as Ethiopian troops were distracted fighting with the Tigray rebels. The Sudan-Ethiopia tensions may not have gained much attention, but if ignored, they could escalate further and lead to mass displacements of people, Raymond’s Yale group said.

articles.title: Ecuador's president denies US operates military base despite reports of troop buildup
articles.summary: Ecuadorian President Daniel Noboa denies the U.S. operates a military base at Taura Air Base, describing American personnel's activities as temporary.
articles.body: Ecuadorian President Daniel Noboa denied that the United States operates a military base in his country after an Agence France-Presse (AFP) investigation signaled an expanded U.S. military presence at an air base near the port city of Guayaquil. "Sometimes there's a specific mission. Sometimes there's a specific operation," Noboa told the news outlet Altavoz, describing U.S. personnel at Taura Air Base as carrying out "temporary activities" under a bilateral security agreement, including intelligence-gathering drone flights. "We work together. It's not an American base. It's an Ecuadoran base," he commented. THE UNLIKELY SOUTH AMERICAN ALLY HELPING LEAD TRUMP'S DRUG CARTEL CRACKDOWN Noboa's remarks came about a month after AFP had documented an unusual deployment of U.S. military aircraft, dozens of tents and construction of new infrastructure at the air base. The investigation identified approximately 20 U.S. military flights arriving at Taura between June and mid-October, along with internal documents confirming the presence of American troops. Several flights originated from U.S. military installations, including Marine Corps Air Station Cherry Point in North Carolina and Dover Air Force Base in Delaware, with stopovers in Puerto Rico and Panama. The buildup also raised legal concerns among senior Ecuadorian military officials. AFP cited a September letter in which then-Air Force commander Gen. Mauricio Salazar asked military leaders to clarify the legality of the deployment. Salazar was subsequently removed from his post and reassigned to a less senior role, the report said. The increased U.S. military presence comes after Ecuadorian voters rejected a Noboa-backed referendum in November 2025 that would have amended the country's constitution to lift its ban on foreign military bases. US MILITARY BOARDS, SEARCHES AND SINKS VESSEL ALLEGEDLY SUPPORTING LOS CHONEROS NARCO-TERRORISTS Despite the referendum's defeat, Quito and Washington have deepened security cooperation to combat drug trafficking and transnational organized crime. Human Rights Watch has described the United States as Ecuador's primary security partner in its crackdown on organized crime, providing equipment, training, intelligence and direct military support. The watchdog characterized the partnership as "perilous," warning that "both governments have engaged in serious human rights violations fuelled by their insistence on framing their confrontations with organised crime groups as a kind of war." Since returning to the White House in January 2025, President Donald Trump has designated several Latin American cartels as foreign terrorist organizations and authorized military strikes against vessels in international waters suspected of drug trafficking. WHITE HOUSE HIGHLIGHTS 'STEEPEST' EVER DECLINE IN US CASUALTIES FROM CARTELS AMID BOAT STRIKES Ecuador has also emerged as a key ally in Trump's crackdown on drug cartels and narcoterrorism, with U.S. and Ecuadorian forces working together to intercept narcotics shipments and dismantle transnational criminal networks, the country's foreign minister told Fox News Digital in September. Roberto Kury said closer cooperation with Washington had delivered "a lot of positive results" in recent months, citing drug shipments intercepted through U.S. intelligence and joint operations. "There is an intelligence (sic) and cooperation from the United States, but there is also always the presence of Ecuadorian military or police. They work together," Kury told Fox News Digital on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly. "Most of the drugs go to the United States. So that’s why the United States shares the problem," Kury said. articles.title: Paraguay’s ousted president moved to military prison after reports of gym and suite in custody
articles.summary: ASUNCIÓN, Paraguay — A Paraguayan judge on Monday ordered former President Santiago Peña moved out of a suite with a private gym and into a military prison as he awaits trial over the collapse of a major digital bank that toppled his government earlier this month.
articles.body: ASUNCIÓN, Paraguay — A Paraguayan judge on Monday ordered former President Santiago Peña moved out of a suite with a private gym and into a military prison as he awaits trial over the collapse of a major digital bank that toppled his government earlier this month. Judge Osmar Legal ordered Peña transferred from the Presidential Escort Regiment, a military base in the capital, Asunción, where photos published by local media showed that his quarters also included a private bathroom, well-furnished office and spacious dining area. Under the court order, a copy of which was obtained by The Associated Press, Peña will be held at the Viñas Cué military prison, apart from other detainees. He arrived there Monday afternoon, his 48th birthday, in handcuffs, a helmet and a bulletproof vest. President Pedro Alliana opened a news conference Monday by announcing that he had ordered the dismissal of the regiment’s commander, Col. José David Daiub, following allegations that Peña had received special treatment there. Alliana, who served as Peña’s vice president, pledged to give prosecutors whatever resources they need to investigate the bank’s collapse. “Paraguayans deserve to know the truth,” he said. Peña is in pretrial detention on charges including breach of trust, criminal association and administration for personal gain. Prosecutors allege that he used his influence to steer public money to Ueno Bank, a lender used by more than half of Paraguay’s adults, as its executives made large insider loans to companies linked to the bank’s owners. The criminal association charge, added Friday, alleges that he led an organization that shielded Ueno from oversight. Peña denies wrongdoing. Paraguay’s central bank eventually seized Ueno on Nov. 3 after declaring it insolvent, freezing the accounts of nearly 3 million customers and more than $850 million in public funds, and disrupting payments for households and small businesses. Three days later, the Senate removed Peña from office, and Alliana took over. A judge ordered Peña jailed the next day. A bank too close to power Ueno’s dizzying growth had become a symbol of Peña’s effort to sell landlocked Paraguay to foreign investors as a low-tax, business-friendly hub. A former International Monetary Fund official and one of the Trump administration’s closest allies in the region, Peña enjoyed prime access to Washington and Wall Street despite his country’s limited economic and geopolitical weight. The bank launched its digital brand in 2022 and by June had 2.9 million customers in a country of about 6 million. It even sponsored the national soccer team. But Ueno was also intertwined with Peña’s government. He held a stake in Ueno’s parent company until last year and appointed the bank’s former chairman, Carlos Carvallo, to lead the central bank. Carvallo, who also faces charges in the case, has said through his lawyer that he did not take part in regulatory decisions involving Ueno. Since Peña’s arrest, authorities have searched two of his four homes, one in Asunción and a mansion in the resort town of San Bernardino, about 50 kilometers (30 miles) away. On Thursday, prosecutors also raided the presidential residence. Prosecutors say the mansion was built partly with about $577,000 in loans that Ueno granted Peña while he was president, and investigators found a vault hidden behind a false wall there. They have also asked the United States, Luxembourg and Argentina for help tracing money that may have been diverted from the bank. Savers left waiting Alliana acknowledged that the crisis had shaken Paraguayans’ faith in their banks. “The closure of Ueno Bank has deeply affected numerous Paraguayan families,” he said. More than 1.8 million depositors have so far received about $640 million, Alliana said, from a deposit guarantee fund that Paraguay created in 2003 after a series of financial crises wiped out dozens of banks and finance companies. Most small savers have been repaid in full. The fund has paid out up to about $19,600 per person, out of a guarantee of about $36,700, and authorities haven’t said when the rest will be paid. Investors in Ueno’s mutual funds aren’t covered and must wait for the bank to be liquidated. Still, more than 75% of the roughly $2.8 billion deposited at Ueno, much of it belonging to larger savers and public institutions, has yet to be returned. For pension funds that had money at Ueno, Alliana said that authorities have preliminarily identified about $600 million in viable assets at the bank, such as loans expected to be repaid, that they plan to use to reimburse the funds. It remains unclear how much of the pension money and other public deposits will be returned. Teachers walked off the job and blocked roads across the country last week to demand the return of their retirement savings, and retirees’ groups have pressed Alliana and Congress to pass an emergency law to guarantee it. That followed days of unrest in Asunción after Ueno’s collapse, when thousands of people took to the streets demanding their money back and Peña’s ouster, at times clashing with police.

articles.title: 36-hour water cut in parts of Navi Mumbai today
articles.summary: NAVI MUMBAI: Water supply to Panvel, parts of Cidco areas, JNPA, Central Railway's Panvel station and 12 gram panchayats will be suspended for 36 hours
articles.body: NAVI MUMBAI: Water supply to Panvel, parts of Cidco areas, JNPA, Central Railway's Panvel station and 12 gram panchayats will be suspended for 36 hours from Tuesday 9am to Wednesday 9pm due to a shutdown by Maharashtra Jeevan Pradhikaran (MJP) to execute seven major works. Areas already facing Cidco's 15% water cut, including Karanjade, are likely to face additional hardship.During the shutdown, MJP will install a steel net at the Vayal water drawal point on the Patalganga river in Khalapur taluka. The affected consumers receive water under the Nhava Sheva Water Supply Scheme Phase-I.The works include electrical repairs, replacement of old pipelines at Lodhivali and along the Mumbai-Pune Expressway, electrical and other works at the Bhokarpada water treatment plant, work on a 12 MLD reservoir, and completion of pending work at New Panvel. MJP deputy engineer RT Waidande has warned that water supply will be at low pressure for two consecutive days, Thursday and Friday, after the shutdown. He has urged consumers to store adequate water in advance and use it judiciously. Cidco has already imposed water cuts in several nodes, including Karanjade, New Panvel (W) and Kalundre.
